1:
The instruments are examined closely. Ellicott makes the first a stylus for engraving stone or metal, and says the second word names the hardness of the diamond rather than its brilliancy, being elsewhere rendered adamant, and meaning strictly the diamond point engravers set in iron. Keil and Delitzsch derive it from a root meaning to scratch, used elsewhere of a fingernail, and distribute the clauses: the table of the heart belongs with the pen of iron, the horns of the altars with the diamond point. They also fix what the sin is: not a proneness to sin but the sinful practice, stamped deep and firmly.

The horns Wesley explains: the altar was foursquare with a rising piece of brass at each corner, and the sin may be engraven there because the blood of sacrifices to idols was sprinkled on them, or because the altars carried an inscription naming the idol. Ellicott adds that the altars may be those of the false worship or of the true they had polluted.

Calvin turns the figure into a measure of degree. Men often fall, and God is ever inclined to mercy; they are led astray by levity, so that their sins are not engraven on their hearts, and while they are lightly besprinkled with vices a remedy remains. But when iniquities are cut into the heart, the marrow and the bones, what more is left? Henry gets there through the courtroom: they had asked what their iniquity was, as though nothing could be charged worth speaking of, and the indictment is proved, too plain to be denied and too bad to be excused, on record in God's omniscience and in their own conscience alike.

One clause about the children is read two ways, and Ellicott decides. Gill reports a rendering, received by a Jewish commentator, that makes it a comparison, as they remember their children so their altars, and presses it further, that they loved their idols better than their offspring, whom they made pass through the fire. Ellicott names that construction and prefers the other, that the children do the remembering, as more natural and better supported by the versions; and he allows that if age is meant, such spectacles may have burnt themselves into the minds of boys who saw them. Calvin, Clarke and Wesley take the children as the rememberers, Calvin adding the point he thinks the interpreters missed, that the iniquity ran down to posterity by a kind of hereditary right, the fathers leaving their children the memorials of their own superstitions.

Whose mountain it is divides them. Gill allows either the temple, called the mountain of the house, or the city on a hill in the midst of a plain. Clarke takes the mountainous land, though the city itself may be meant. Ellicott makes it a poetic name for Zion, whose greatness lies not in rising above the country round but in being the mountain of Jehovah. Calvin alone refuses the vocative: it seems appropriate at first sight, but the context is a people who always ran to their recesses when afraid, so the sense is that the mountains shall be as the fields, and no hiding-place will serve.

The word for discontinuing carries the law with it, and two hear it. Keil and Delitzsch trace it to the statutes about letting the ground lie untilled in the seventh year and releasing what has been lent, and read the sentence as an answer in kind: because Judah broke that law, the Lord will make them loose their hold of the inheritance. Ellicott calls the word half-technical for the same practices and completes the irony: the land would now have its rest and enjoy its sabbaths, though the people had failed in the obedience prescribed. Calvin makes the loss worse than death, since some would remain alive and be scattered, perishing living and seeing.
5:
The curse is read as diagnosis. Ellicott calls the words vehement and abrupt, bursting out as a naming of the root evil that had eaten into the people's life, since trust in an arm of flesh produced the Egyptian and Assyrian alliances and these the departing from the Lord; he notes too that two different words stand behind the English man, the first implying strength and the second weakness. Calvin hears the second as contemptuous, the Hebrews commonly saying the same thing twice. Clarke narrows it to Egypt, too feeble and too ill-disposed to help heartily, then widens it: whoever trusts an arm of flesh for the salvation of his soul, whether himself or another or anything he has done, inherits a curse instead of a blessing.

Why the sentence stands here Calvin and Keil and Delitzsch answer differently. Calvin thinks the prophet prefixed it to many discourses and wrote once for all what he had often said, since he found promises and threatenings alike disregarded and dealt with a proud people who, relying on their own defences, rejected what came under God's authority. Keil and Delitzsch map it instead: the section runs to the eighteenth verse on the sources of ruin and of well-being, and thence to the end on the way to life, the curse and the blessing paired and the prophet's prayer attached.

Henry treats the passage as a practical sermon rather than a prophecy, of which we probably have only the heads. The man is cursed for the affront, or cursed in the sense of miserable, since he leans on a broken reed that will not only fail him but run into his hand and pierce it. The sin is placing in the wisdom, power and faithfulness of men the confidence that belongs to those attributes in God alone, treating as principal agents what are only instruments.

On the word flesh Henry presses every sense: weak as flesh without bone or sinew, inactive as flesh without spirit, mortal as flesh that soon corrupts, and false besides. The malignity is that this is the evil heart of unbelief departing from the living God, for men may call him their hope with the mouth while the heart withdraws, and cleaving to the cistern is leaving the fountain. The outcome is a cheat put on oneself: when good comes he shall not see it, and when the times mend they will not mend with him.

What the shrub is nobody can settle. Gill runs the versions, rejects a rendering making it something thorny without and eatable within, and takes it for ling or heath, a low shrub of waste ground, fruitless and seedless and reckoned by the naturalist among the unhappy plants forbidden for sacred use. Clarke abandons the shrub for a blasted tree, parched and withered, and adds a physiology for the next clause: it will not be sensible of good coming, the drought having left it unable to absorb more juices. Calvin reports the Jewish guesses of juniper and tamarisk, rejects the juniper since fruit grows on its branches, and concludes only that it was a useless shrub now unknown.

Ellicott sets out the whole choice and decides it on literary grounds. The word means literally bare or naked and is rendered destitute elsewhere, a sense some recent commentators adopt, and no picture of desolation could be more complete than a destitute man inhabiting the parched places. But all the older versions take it for a shrub standing alone in barren ground, and a like word means juniper in Arabic. Both are tenable; the shrub is the bolder similitude and balances the tree planted by the waters in the verse that follows, which is more after the manner of a poet-prophet. And he gives the reason plainly: there is something weak in saying that a man shall be like a destitute man.
7:
The beatitude is heard against a psalm. Ellicott says the description that follows is almost a paraphrase of the first psalm and was probably suggested by it, and gives the arrangement a name: the prophet has his own Ebal and Gerizim, trust inheriting the blessing and distrust the curse. Keil and Delitzsch call it an extension of the same picture. Calvin notices the order rather than the source, that the prophet could not have taught this second part profitably without first pulling up the false confidence, since seed cast on uncultivated soil bears nothing and the plough must go before the seed.

The tree is worked against the shrub. Clarke explains the mechanism: roots spread by the river absorb all the moisture the tree needs, however intense the heat and long the drought. Calvin sets the two side by side: the tamarisk has the appearance of life but no moisture in a dry soil, so its roots quickly dry. Gill turns it christological, a tree planted not by ministers who plant and water instrumentally but by the Lord as efficient cause, in Christ and in the likeness of his death and resurrection. Ellicott stays with a word: another reading gives shall not fear, but repeating the same verb as in the earlier verse has more force, and yields the chiasm he draws out, that as the blasted heath sees no good, so the tree sees no evil.

One word about the heart divides them three ways. Clarke says the received rendering is simply wrong, since the Hebrew is never used in Scripture to denote wickedness of any kind and means rather wretched or feeble, distressed beyond all things; he cites a lexicographer and an old English version that has, shrewd is the heart of a man, and unsearchable. Ellicott renders it incurably diseased, and explains what is preserved and what given up: wickedness is implied, but as a moral taint following the deliberate choice rather than the choice itself. Wesley keeps the strong word and adds the double unsearchableness, that a man cannot know his own heart nor any other know his neighbour's.

Why the heart matters here they set out differently. Ellicott supplies the logic of the sequence: if blessing and curse are so plainly marked, how does a man come to choose the curse, and the answer lies in a self-deceit that blinds his perception of good and evil. Gill makes it the source of the idolatry and creature-confidence already charged, and describes the fraud, since the heart proposes sin under the notion of pleasure and promises much it does not yield, all fancy and illusion, short-lived and ending in bitterness. Calvin warns against the use commonly made of the verse: many lay hold of the words and mutilate them without regard to the design, whereas one ought first to see what the prophet had in view and what necessity led him to speak, and only then draw the general doctrine.

The answer to the question is where two argue from grammar and one from doctrine. Ellicott notes that the Hebrew has the singular, his way, and that the interpolated conjunction is better dropped, so that the closing words explain what went before; Keil and Delitzsch defend that same conjunction, absent from many manuscripts and from the old translators, on the ground that it sets the aim apart and gives it the prominence of an independent thought. Gill argues instead from exclusiveness: none but Jehovah can search a heart so, and since Christ is said to search the reins and to discern the thoughts, he must be Jehovah. Clarke observes that the apostles called him the Knower of the heart, a title applicable to him alone; and Calvin adds the general truth, that the recesses of the heart are so hidden that no human being can form a judgment of another man.
11:
What the bird does divides them, and one of them checks it against nature. Ellicott renders it heaps up eggs and has not laid them, and reports the popular Jewish belief behind it, that the partridge steals other birds' eggs and adds them to her own, so that the broods desert her when they hatch; the parable is then of the covetous man piling up riches not rightly his. He adds honestly that modern naturalists have not observed the habit, and suggests the belief arose from the cuckoo laying in the partridge's nest. Clarke reports two translators to the same effect, one of whom draws the moral that the young, when able to shift for themselves, abandon a bird that is not their mother. Gill and Wesley take the other construction, of eggs sat on and never hatched, lost by accident or taken by man or beast.

The end of the covetous man they render differently. Calvin takes the last word to mean a thing of nought, so that the man becomes a mockery, and notes that some render it fool. Clarke keeps the fool and adds that he shall be reputed such, having been one all the way through, since he lost his soul to get wealth and never enjoyed it. Wesley makes the folly retrospective: he shall lose it again before he dies, and then understand what a fool he was.

Henry explains the shape of the passage rather than its parts. The prophet is retired for private meditation and alone with God, which is what ministers who would have comfort in their work must often be; and in that converse he takes the liberty devout souls use in soliloquy, passing from one thing to another without tying himself strictly to the laws of method and coherence. Keil and Delitzsch reach the same estimate by another route, preferring to read the throne as an apostrophe because that suits the tension of feeling in the discourse.

How the words about the throne stand is a grammatical question with three answers. Ellicott would join the verse to the next and drop the supplied verb, so that the nouns are all vocatives addressed to God: thou throne of glory on high from the beginning, the place of our sanctuary, the hope of Israel. Keil and Delitzsch report the older commentators who take it as a plain statement, allow that this is grammatically defensible, and side with the moderns for the apostrophe; they also fix the place of the sanctuary as the temple and not heaven. Gill passes on a Jewish reading that supplies a particle of comparison, making the temple like a glorious high throne, with heaven as the throne itself.

Being written in the earth is read three ways. Clarke makes it erasure, the names written in dust so that the first wind blowing over will mar every letter. Ellicott makes it a contrast with a name graven on rock for ever, and recovers the vividness by the eastern habit of writing on the ground, familiar from a memorable instance in the gospel and from the common practice of Jewish schools. Wesley makes it portion rather than record, that such shall have nothing beyond the earth.

Calvin ties the praise to the charge. It becomes clear here why the excellency of the nation was commended first: the comparison was to make their impiety less excusable, since the more bountifully God dealt with them the more atrocious was the ingratitude. What does it avail you, he asks in their name, that God dwells among you and the temple is as it were his earthly habitation, when no one accepts the favour? And he adds why Scripture rehearses blessings at all, with a twofold object, to persuade us that he who begins will finish, and to move us to render thanks.
14:
What the prophet asks to be healed of they answer three ways. Gill takes it of his own sins and his share in a corrupt time, sins being diseases and their healing forgiveness, or else of the wound his people's sins had made in him. Ellicott makes it a contrast, conscious or not, with the deserters just described: he needs healing and salvation like them, but knows where to seek it and is sure the work will not be left incomplete. Calvin makes it self-preservation, the prophet hiding under the wings of God because apostasy prevailed everywhere and every turn offered what would allure him away. Clarke and Wesley keep to the last clause, that the whole glory of the work belongs to God alone.

The mockers' question yields a date. Ellicott observes that the speakers are unnamed but are plainly those who questioned his prophetic character because his threats had gone unfulfilled, and infers that the words were written before the king's death and the capture of the city; he adds that the closing particle is the usual formula of request and carries the sneer, let it come, if you please. Clarke answers from history: no such events had yet taken place, but they did, and every tittle of the menace was strictly fulfilled. Calvin diagnoses the misuse of forbearance common among the reprobate, who counted the years of quiet as a refutation.

One clause about the shepherd is read four ways. Gill takes it that he had not been importunate to be dismissed from a service that earned him such usage. Clarke follows a translator who gives, I have not been in haste to outrun thy guidance, and glosses it that for the credit of his prophecy he had not wished the calamity quickly but pleaded for respite. Wesley balances it, that he neither sought the office nor declined it when called. Ellicott calls the English obscure and offers, I have not been quick to withdraw from my work in following thee, then reports a bolder possibility, that the shepherding is literal and the parallel is with the herdsman-prophet, and conjectures, admitting it is no more than conjecture, that before his call he may have been employed in the pasture grounds of his priestly town.

The next petition divides Clarke from the rest. Gill, Ellicott and Calvin take the terror to be desertion, God withdrawing his presence or leaving the message unfulfilled and the messenger a by-word, which Ellicott says would make the prophetic work more terrible than ever, and which Calvin defines as a dread that stupefies all the feelings. Clarke reads it as a plea against the commission itself: do not command me to predict miseries and then abandon me to them and to my enemies.

The curse on the persecutors Clarke defuses and Calvin justifies. Clarke says the words are to be understood as simple predictions rather than prayers, so that they shall be confounded rather than let them be. Calvin lets the prayer stand and explains the standing: the quarrel was not with one man or a few but with the whole people, and probably with several parties at once, since crying out against the avaricious raised all who lived by plunder, speaking against lust raised a second conspiracy, and condemning drunkenness a third; having no private concern in it, he could pray against men who had shown themselves the declared enemies of God.

Two smaller notes close the prayer. Ellicott renders the last words literally, break them with a twofold breaking, and hears the psalmist behind the petition. Keil and Delitzsch ground the whole entreaty on one thing, that the Lord should not bring his prophet to shame by leaving the prophecies against Judah unfulfilled, which is also his encouragement to pray at all, God being his refuge in the day of evil.
19:
That a new discourse begins they all say, and one with irritation. Gill calls it a fresh sermon on the sanctifying of the sabbath and a very proper place to have begun a new chapter; Calvin agrees and adds that whoever divided the chapters was deficient in judgment here as in many other places. Ellicott makes it the opening of a fresh series, arranged probably in chronological order and reported with much fuller circumstances. On when it was delivered he and Henry both argue from the promises attached and reach different reigns: Henry places it under the reforming king, since such promises are scarcely found when matters come nearer the extremity, while Ellicott refers it to the early years of the reign that followed, before the sins had taken the hopeless character of the previous chapters.

Which gate is meant nobody can fix. Clarke takes simply the most public one, of the greatest thoroughfare. Ellicott points out that no gate so described appears in the great topographical record or elsewhere, so conjecture is all that is left, and infers from the context a place of concourse belonging to the temple rather than the city. Henry explains why gates at all: not only because people were continually passing, but because the courts were kept and the stores laid up there; and the proclamation begins, as a king's does, at the court gate.

Calvin raises the objection the passage invites and answers it. Resting one day seems a small matter; God declares elsewhere that he does not care for such outward worship, hypocrites reckoning their duty done when they have kept the seventh day, and bodily exercise profits little. Why then is the neglect reproved so severely? Because these men were not hypocrites about it: they violated the day openly, grown so lost as to pretend no religion and feel no shame; and if that was the state of the capital, what must have been done in the obscure villages? Clarke supplies the consequence rather than the defence: the breach of the sabbath led to neglect of sacrifice, of the ordinances and of all public worship, and so brought all immorality with it, letting in the whole flood of wrath.

Two phrases are narrowed. On taking heed to yourselves, Calvin rejects the rendering as your lives are precious to you, and takes the word for the affections of the heart, so that the charge is to lay this up inwardly; Gill reads it the same way, of a mind disposed for the work of the day and not taken up with other cares. On the burden, Gill refuses to restrict it, as some do, to dirt and soil, and extends it to any ware carried out to be sold. Ellicott fills in the traffic from a later parallel: baskets of fruit and fish brought in by villagers coming up to the services, and the city's wares taken to the gates to be sold to them in turn. The day was kept after a fashion, he says, but turned into a market, so that men abstained from manual labour while its quiet sanctity was lost.

The appeal to the fathers Calvin turns round. The crime is aggravated, not excused, by being old: the sabbath had been violated by the fathers already, and children are less excusable for following bad examples, though the world does not commonly think so, since most men boast of those examples when they wish to reject the Law and the Prophets and the gospel, and reckon themselves behind a strong shield when they can answer that the fathers did otherwise. Gill says the same briefly: the command was disobeyed very early and more or less ever since. Clarke adds a textual note on the summons itself, that eight manuscripts and two versions omit the clause naming all Judah beside the kings.
24:
The turn to promise they all mark. Gill reads the opening as a concession, that so it shall be notwithstanding all former disobedience. Clarke draws the general rule from it, that though destruction had been positively threatened there was an unexpressed proviso throughout, and a succession of princes would have continued had they returned. Calvin puts the offer in the prophet's mouth: your fathers provoked vengeance for ages, but as God is ever inclined to mercy he is ready to forgive if only you cease to follow them.

Calvin then asks the question the promise invites: was resting on the seventh day of such moment that the perpetuity of a kingdom should hang on it? His answer is that the outward rite carried a spiritual end, the day being commanded as a visible symbol of their own sanctification, so that the observance meant is not the naked rite but something greater, a learning by self-denial to render themselves up to God.

What is promised falls into two parts. Calvin takes kingdom and priesthood together as the whole of their happiness, both being types of Christ, since by the one they knew God propitious and by the other that he was the guardian of their safety. Ellicott hears the plural of kings and princes as giving vividness and grandeur to a picture of revived majesty, and perhaps as marking that it would endure. On the places named he turns topographer: the plain is the lowland stretching to the sea, the mountain the hill-country, the south the region below Hebron, and each name, though descriptive in sense, was used as definitely as we use the Campagna of Rome or the Weald of Kent. The offerings he sorts as well, distinguishing those wholly consumed on the altar from those of which the flesh was eaten.

The threat that closes the sermon they take with different force. Keil and Delitzsch state it plainly, that if the desecration continues the city is to be burnt with fire. Ellicott holds the fire figurative rather than literal, the fierce anger of the Lord that man cannot quench, of which an actual conflagration may have been the instrument. Calvin explains the order of the two, that God first kindly allures and then, finding men refractory, deals with them according to the hardness of their hearts; and he narrows the entering to the transaction of business, since going out of the city was itself lawful. Clarke leaves the responsibility where the sermon leaves it: their sin lay at their own door, so fully were they warned and so basely did they reject the counsel of God against themselves.
